messages.content: Some of my cassava plants are very short and have pale, mottled leaves, should I keep them?

No, those plants are infected with cassava mosaic disease and must be removed. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next planting, select cuttings only from plants with normal green leaves and no deformation. Get tolerant, clean cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. This will keep your new stand uniform and well-fed. For clean cuttings, see ITRA.
What is African cassava mosaic virus and how do I manage it?

African cassava mosaic virus causes cassava mosaic disease, which shows yellow or pale mottling and twisted leaves. No spray can cure an infected plant, so uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants. For the next planting, take cuttings ONLY from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.
how to avoid cassava mosaic spread

Use only healthy cuttings and plant a tolerant variety. First, uproot and destroy any strongly mottled or stunted plants because they will not recover and feed the whitefly spread. Then, for the next planting, select cuttings only from plants with normal green leaves and no leaf distortion; never cut from a mottled or deformed stem. After you have clean cuttings, plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer to keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need help identifying healthy cuttings, go to ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.
why must I destroy mottled plants

Destroying strongly mottled, stunted plants stops the main way the disease moves. Those plants are infected and will not recover, and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. After removal, you take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants, which prevents planting infected cuttings. Then you plant a tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered producer to keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For confirmation of plant health you can consult ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.
is it bacterial blight if leaves are twisted

It is not bacterial blight; twisted, puckered or shrunken leaves are a sign of cassava mosaic disease, not bacterial blight. Bacterial blight shows angular water-soaked spots with wilting and shoot die-back, without leaf deformation. To tell them apart, look for leaf distortion: if the leaves are twisted or pale mottled, it is mosaic; if you see angular spots and wilting but the leaves stay normal, it is bacterial blight. For mosaic, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled plants, then take cuttings only from healthy plants and plant a tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. If you see angular spots with wilting, go to ICAT to confirm.
what dose of pesticide kills cassava mosaic virus

There is no spray that cures an infected cassava plant, so a pesticide dose will not eliminate the virus. The steps are to uproot and destroy any strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and feed the whitefly spread. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem, and plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer to keep a uniform, well-fed stand.
My cassava leaves look strange, what should I do?
Do the leaves show yellow mottling and twisted shape, or angular water-soaked spots with wilting?
They are yellow mottled and twisted.

You have cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and will keep feeding the whitefly. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer to reduce the risk. Keep a uniform, well-fed stand so the field stays strong. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.
I have a few chickens that survived a sudden death outbreak. Can I take them to market?

No, you must not move, sell or give any bird after a Newcastle disease outbreak. First isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones. Then burn or bury all dead birds and the soiled litter. Disinfect the house thoroughly. Finally vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in drinking water or as eye-drops and follow the vaccination schedule. If you need help, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately.
Many of my chickens died all at once and the rest look fine. Should I still take the healthy ones to the market?

No, you must not move, sell or give any bird after a sudden mass death. Burn or bury the dead birds and any soiled litter. Disinfect the house. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in drinking water or as eye-drops and repeat as scheduled. See the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary right away.
My chickens are coughing and then several died suddenly; can I still transport the remaining birds?

No, you must not move, sell or give any bird after those signs. Isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones. Burn or bury the dead birds and any contaminated litter. Disinfect the house. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in drinking water or as eye-drops and keep to the vaccination schedule. Contact the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary immediately.
How should I handle a flock infected with Newcastle disease virus?

Newcastle disease virus requires you to keep all birds on the farm; do not move, sell or gift any bird. First isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones. Then burn or bury dead birds and the soiled litter and disinfect the house. After that vaccinate the flock with the La Sota (or B1) strain in drinking water or as eye-drops, repeating on the recommended schedule. For assistance, see the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.
Can I take sick chickens to market?

No, you must not move, sell or give any bird that shows signs of Newcastle disease. First isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones to stop spread. Then burn or bury all dead birds and any soiled litter, and disinfect the house thoroughly. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain by adding it to the drinking water or applying it as eye-drops, and keep to the repeat schedule. Finally, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away for further help.
My birds have sudden deaths, so it must be fowl pox, I will just burn the dead and move the rest to market.

It is not fowl pox, it is Newcastle disease. Newcastle causes older birds to die suddenly in large numbers, while fowl pox shows scabs or lesions and progresses more slowly. Because it is Newcastle, you must not move, sell or give any bird. Isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones, then burn or bury all dead birds and any soiled litter and disinfect the house. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in drinking water or as eye-drops and repeat on schedule. See the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary immediately.
I have some chickens that I want to take to the market, but I'm not sure if it's safe.
Are many of your birds dying suddenly?
Yes, several died at once and the others look fine.

You are dealing with Newcastle disease, which causes sudden mass deaths in older birds. Isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones and do NOT move, sell or gift any bird. Burn or bury the dead birds and any soiled litter, then disinfect the house thoroughly. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop and repeat the vaccination on the recommended schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately for help.
When should I first open my new beehives and how often should I check them?

Open the first hive about ~8 days after the bees have settled. Then visit each hive every 8 days. Always wear full protective gear and use a lit smoker when you open the hive. Place the hives where nectar plants grow, under light shade, sheltered from wind and rain, on four tar-coated pillars, and rub the inside with citronella attractant. For further help, see an experienced beekeeper or ITRA/ICAT Sotouboua for hive choice and disease.
I have just set up a few hives near my garden where the flowers bloom. The bees are inside now. What should I do next and how often should I check them?

You should open the first hive about ~8 days after the bees settled inside. After that, visit each hive every 8 days. When you open a hive, wear full protective gear and light a smoker. Keep the hives where nectar plants grow, under light shade, sheltered from wind and rain, on four tar-coated pillars, and rub the inside with citronella attractant. If you need advice on hive choice or disease, consult an experienced beekeeper or ITRA/ICAT Sotouboua.
first opening when, check interval?

Open the first hive about ~8 days after the bees have settled. Then check each hive every 8 days. Always wear full protective gear and use a lit smoker when you open the hive. Place the hives where nectar plants grow, under light shade, sheltered from wind and rain, on four tar-coated pillars, and rub the inside with citronella attractant. For advice on hive choice or disease, see an experienced beekeeper or ITRA/ICAT Sotouboua.
What exact time of day should I open the hive for the first time and how many minutes should I smoke it?

You should open the first hive about ~8 days after the bees have settled, then visit every 8 days, always in full gear with a lit smoker. Place the hives where nectar plants grow, under light shade, sheltered from wind and rain, on four tar-coated pillars, and rub the inside with citronella attractant. I cannot give you an exact time of day or the number of minutes to smoke the hive. For those details, ask an experienced beekeeper or ITRA/ICAT Sotouboua.
I just got some new beehives, not sure how often to check them.
Did you already place the hives near nectar plants and protect them from wind?
Yes, I set them under some shade and on the pillars as advised.

The first opening should be done ~8 days after the bees settle in the hive. Place the hives where nectar plants grow, under light shade, sheltered from wind and rain, on four tar-coated pillars, and rub the inside with a swarm attractant such as citronella. After the first opening, visit the hives every 8 days to inspect them. Always wear full protective gear and use a lit smoker when you open the hive. For help choosing the right hive type or diagnosing disease, see an experienced beekeeper or ITRA/ICAT Sotouboua.
I have a small piece of land on the Plateaux Ouest with good soil and I want to start a cacao plot. What steps should I follow?

First, confirm that your land receives between 1,200 and 2,000 mm of rain per year and has rich, deep, well-drained soil at least 80 to 100 cm deep. Secure long-term land rights before you begin. Then, set a provisional shade of banana and later plant permanent agroforestry shade at a spacing of 12 by 10 metres, which gives about 90 trees per hectare. Plant your cacao seedlings in June or July. Each month, protect the apex of each tree from psyllids and caterpillars and the base from termites. Before the dry season, create a firebreak around the plot. For planting material and the shade system, see ICAT or ITRA.
I want to start a cacao farm but I am not sure what steps I need to follow.
Which month are you planning to plant your cacao seedlings?
I plan to plant in July.

You should protect the apex of each tree every month against psyllids and caterpillars and protect the base against termites, and you must make a firebreak before the dry season. First choose a plot that receives 1,200-2,000 mm of rain per year, has rich, deep, well-drained soil at least 80-100 cm deep, and secure long-term land rights. Then set a provisional shade of banana and later establish a permanent agroforestry shade at 12 by 10 metres, about 90 trees per hectare. Plant your seedlings in June-July as you plan, following the shade system you have prepared. After planting, carry out the monthly protection of the apex and base as described and create the firebreak before the dry season starts. For planting material and advice on the shade system, contact ICAT or ITRA.
How can I stop cassava bacterial blight from spreading in my field?

Use cuttings only from healthy plants. Remove and destroy any affected plants you see. Disinfect your tools between each plant. If you need clean resistant cuttings, go to ITRA or a registered producer. To be sure of the disease, you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
My cassava leaves have angular water-soaked spots and the young leaves are wilting, and some stems are oozing gum. What should I do?

Do not use any cuttings from those plants. Remove and destroy the affected plants right away. Disinfect your tools before moving to the next plant. Choose cuttings only from plants that look healthy. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot to a different site. For clean resistant cuttings you can visit ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can help confirm the disease.
I see my cassava shoots dying back after the leaves wilt and there is gum on the stems. How can I manage this problem?

Stop using any cuttings from the dying shoots. Pull out and destroy those plants. Clean and disinfect all tools between each plant. Take new cuttings only from plants that have no wilting or gum. Get clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer and ask ICAT to check the diagnosis.
What steps should I follow to control Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis in my cassava farm?

The disease is called cassava bacterial blight. Use cuttings only from healthy plants. Remove and destroy any affected plants you find. Disinfect your tools between each plant. For clean resistant cuttings go to ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
my cassava has angular spots, it's mosaic so I take cuttings from healthy side

It is not cassava mosaic, it is bacterial blight caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. Mosaic shows yellow mottling and leaf deformation without wilting, while blight gives angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves, shoot die-back, and sometimes gum on stems. Because it is blight, you must not rely only on taking cuttings from the apparently healthy side. Use cuttings only from plants that have no spots, no wilting, and no gum. Remove and destroy every plant showing the blight symptoms. Disinfect your tools between each plant to stop tool-borne spread. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot for future protection. Have ICAT confirm the diagnosis and get clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer.
My cassava leaves have angular water-soaked spots and the young leaves are wilting, what should I do?

Those signs are cassava bacterial blight, so you must act quickly. First, remove and destroy the affected plants to stop the bacterium from staying in the field. Disinfect your tools between each plant before you move to the next one. Use cuttings only from healthy plants when you replant. For clean resistant cuttings, visit ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
I see gum coming out of the stems and the shoots are dying back, what can I do?

Gum exuding on stems and shoot die-back are also signs of cassava bacterial blight. Remove and destroy those plants immediately. Disinfect your tools between each plant to avoid spreading the bacterium. Only use cuttings from healthy plants for the new planting. For clean resistant cuttings, go to ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
What steps should I follow to control Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis?

The disease caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis is cassava bacterial blight. Use cuttings only from healthy plants and remove and destroy any affected plants. Disinfect tools between each plant to prevent spread. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot with another crop before re-planting cassava. For clean resistant cuttings, contact ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
it is cassava mosaic so I just take healthy cuttings

It is not cassava mosaic, it is bacterial blight. Mosaic shows yellow mottling and leaf deformation without wilting, while blight shows angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves and shoot die-back, sometimes with gum on stems. Because it is blight, you must remove and destroy all affected plants, disinfect tools between each plant, and only use cuttings from healthy plants. Get clean resistant cuttings from ITRA and have ICAT confirm the diagnosis.
when should I plant the resistant variety after rotation

Plant the resistant variety after you have removed and destroyed all diseased plants and disinfected your tools. Then, clean all tools with a disinfectant before handling new cuttings. Choose a resistant cassava variety from a registered producer and plant it in the rotated plot, keeping it away from previous cassava locations. I cannot give you an exact planting date, and you should ask ITRA for timing advice and ICAT for any further diagnosis help.
My cassava leaves are looking sick and the plants are dying.
Are the spots on the leaves angular and water-soaked with wilting of young leaves?
Yes, the spots are angular, water-soaked and the young leaves are wilting.

Use cuttings only from healthy plants and discard any cuttings from diseased stems. Remove and destroy all affected plants to stop the bacterium from spreading. Disinfect your tools between each plant to avoid contaminating healthy cuttings. Plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared plot and rotate the plot to a different location for the next season. You should contact ITRA or a registered producer for clean resistant cuttings and ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
I see many of my cowpea flowers falling off and the pods look bored, and there are tiny insects gathering on the shoots.

You have thrips, pod borers and aphids attacking your cowpea field. Sow a resistant improved 55-75 day variety when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. Weed early, doing the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. Spray three times around flowering: first spray when flower buds appear at 30-35 days, second spray ten days later, and third spray ten days after the second, using an approved product at the label rate. Go to ICAT to get the current approved product and the exact dose before you spray.
I see many aphids clustering on my cowpea shoots and some pods look bored.
Do you also notice damaged or dropped flowers on the plants?
Yes, many flowers are damaged and some have dropped.

You have a wave of cowpea pests - flower thrips, pod borers and aphids - that damage flowers, drop them and bore into pods. The insects reinvade in waves, so one spray is not enough. First, sow a resistant improved variety that matures in 55 to 75 days when the rains are strong, around mid-June to early July. Weed early, with the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. Spray three times around flowering: first spray at 30-35 days when flower buds appear, second spray ten days later, and third spray ten days after the second, using an approved product at the label rate. Before spraying, ask ICAT for the current approved product and the exact dose.
What sanitation steps should I follow to avoid groundnut leaf spot?

Do not grow groundnut on the same land year after year, rotate with cereals. Use a tolerant variety and clear or bury old groundnut trash before planting. Harvest your crop on time so a weakened crop does not drop its pods early. These actions break the cycle of the Cercospora leaf-spot fungi that lives in crop residues. If you need advice on resistant varieties or whether a fungicide is needed, go to ICAT.
My groundnut leaves have dark round spots and are turning yellow and falling off early. What should I do?

Those signs are groundnut leaf spot, so you must remove the source of infection. Clear or bury all old groundnut residues from the field before you plant again. Plant a tolerant groundnut variety and do not plant groundnut on that same plot the next season, rotate with cereals instead. Harvest the crop on time to avoid weakened plants dropping pods early. For further help with resistant varieties or fungicide decisions, visit ICAT.
My groundnut plants are dropping leaves early and the leaves look yellow, but I don't see any spots yet.

Early leaf yellowing and drop are also symptoms of groundnut leaf spot. Clear and bury any previous groundnut crop residues in the field. Rotate the field with cereals and avoid planting groundnut on the same land consecutively. Choose a tolerant groundnut variety for the next planting and harvest on time to keep the crop strong. If you need advice on resistant varieties or fungicide use, see ICAT.
How do I manage Cercospora leaf-spot in my groundnut field?

Cercospora leaf-spot is the same as groundnut leaf spot. Do not grow groundnut on the same land year after year; rotate with cereals. Use a tolerant variety and clear or bury old groundnut trash before planting. Harvest on time so a weakened crop does not drop its pods early. For advice on resistant varieties or whether a fungicide is justified, contact ICAT.
my groundnut has rosette, so just rotate cereals

It is not rosette; the symptoms you described are dark, roundish spots on leaves, yellowing and early leaf drop, which match groundnut leaf spot caused by Cercospora fungi. Rosette shows mottling and stunted growth, a viral disease, not the same spots. Because it is leaf spot, you must rotate groundnut with cereals, avoid planting groundnut on the same plot consecutively, use a tolerant variety, clear or bury all old groundnut trash, and harvest on time to prevent pod loss. For resistant variety choices and fungicide advice, see ICAT.
what fungicide dose should I spray for leaf spot

Use a tolerant groundnut variety and rotate with cereals to reduce leaf spot pressure. After each harvest, clear or bury all old groundnut residues so the fungus cannot survive. Harvest your crop on time to avoid early pod drop. I cannot give you the exact fungicide dose, and you should ask ICAT for guidance on whether a fungicide is justified and the correct application rate.
My groundnut leaves are looking sick and the pods are falling early.
Are the leaves showing dark, roundish spots and turning yellow before they drop?
Yes, the leaves have dark round spots and they turn yellow and drop early.

You have groundnut leaf spot caused by Cercospora fungi. Do not grow groundnut on the same land year after year, rotate the field with cereals. Use a tolerant groundnut variety and clear or bury all old groundnut residues before planting. Harvest the crop on time so a weakened plant does not drop its pods early. For resistant varieties and advice on whether a fungicide is needed, consult ICAT.
My maize leaves are turning yellow after a heavy rain. What should I do about nitrogen loss?

The yellowing of the lower leaves after heavy rain is a sign of nitrogen loss. First open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. Then, when the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation and keeping the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT.
After the rain, the bottom leaves of my maize are getting pale from the base upward, but there are no spots. What can I do?

Pale lower leaves after rain indicate nitrogen has been washed away. Open a shallow drainage channel to let water flow off the plot. Once the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping it off the plant to avoid burning. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later notice streaks or dead-hearts, see ICAT.
My maize plants look weak and the leaves near the ground are turning yellow soon after a downpour, but there are no streaks. How should I treat this?

Yellowing of the lower leaves after a heavy rain is caused by nitrogen loss. First, dig a shallow drainage channel so excess water can leave the plot. After drainage, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation and keeping the fertilizer off the plant to prevent burn. Continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as planned. If streaks or dead-hearts appear, consult ICAT.
What is the correct response to nitrogen leaching in maize after heavy rain?

Nitrogen leaching causes the lower leaves to yellow. Open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping it off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you see any streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT.
why leaves yellow after rain

The lower leaves turn yellow because nitrogen has been washed below the young roots by the heavy rain. First open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. Then, once the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping the granules off the plant so they do not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you see any streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT.
my maize has yellow lower leaves after rain, it must be maize streak virus so I will spray pesticide

It is not maize streak virus. Yellowing of the lower leaves from the bottom up with no streaks is a sign of nitrogen loss, not a virus. The virus shows pale streaks along veins, while the pest shows dead-heart symptoms. To treat nitrogen loss, first open a shallow drainage channel to let water run off the plot. After drainage, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping it off the plant. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If streaks or dead-hearts ever appear, see ICAT.
when exactly should I open the drainage after a storm

Open the shallow drainage channel as soon as you notice water standing on the plot after the heavy rain, so the water can run off instead of staying. After the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping the granules off the plant. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. I cannot give you an exact date for opening the channel; the local extension officer can advise you on timing for your specific field.
My maize leaves are turning yellow after the rain.
Did the yellowing start on the lower leaves and spread upward without any spots?
Yes, the lower leaves turned pale first and there are no spots.

The problem is nitrogen loss because waterlogged soil also starves the roots of air. Open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. Once the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see pale streaks on veins or dead-heart symptoms, go to ICAT.
How does the maize stalk borer survive in old stalks and what should I do after harvest?

The stalk borer can live in the old stalks left in the field after harvest. After you finish harvesting, destroy the old stalks or bury them deep so the larvae cannot survive. Then plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same area to break the pest cycle. Rotate or intercrop with the legume immediately after the old stalks are removed. If a large block of your field is attacked at once, go to ICAT quickly for approved control. I cannot give you a specific date for these actions.
My maize plants have holes in the whorl leaves that look like window panes and the centre shoot is dead while the outer leaves are still green. What is happening?

Those signs are typical of maize stalk borer damage. While the plants are still young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel. One kilogram of this mixture will treat about 1,500 to 2,000 plants. Repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days while the crop is still young. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always mix it with the inert carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If many plants are affected at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.
I see a dead central shoot in my maize but the outer leaves are still alive and there are small holes in the whorl leaves. What should I do?

A dead central shoot together with window-pane holes in the whorl leaves indicates maize stalk borer. While the crop is still young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel. One kilogram of this mix covers about 1,500 to 2,000 plants and should be applied every 8 to 10 days. Do not apply neem powder by itself because the oil will scorch the plant; always use the sand or clay carrier. After you harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and plant a legume like cowpea or soybean to rotate the field. If a large area is badly attacked, go to ICAT quickly for approved control.
Is Busseola fusca the same as the stalk borer that makes dead hearts in maize, and how can I manage it?

Busseola fusca is one of the stem borers that causes the dead-heart symptom in maize. To manage it, when the plants are still young drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel; one kilogram treats about 1,500-2,000 plants and you should repeat every 8-10 days. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always mix it with the inert carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.
how stop stalk borer carry over

Destroy or deep-bury old stalks after harvest and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. While the plants are young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel. Use one kilogram of the mixture for about fifteen hundred to two thousand plants and repeat the application every eight to ten days. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly.
It is maize streak, so I just need more fertilizer

It is not maize streak, it is stalk borer causing the dead-heart and window-pane holes. Maize streak shows leaf streaks and pale veins, not tunnels or dead central shoots. To treat borer, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks after harvest and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. While the crop is young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel, using one kilogram for fifteen hundred to two thousand plants and repeat every eight to ten days. Never apply neem powder alone. For a large outbreak, see ICAT quickly.
how many grams of neem powder per plant

Use a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay for each leaf funnel, which treats about fifteen hundred to two thousand plants per kilogram of the mixture. Apply this while the plants are young and repeat every eight to ten days. Never apply neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. I cannot give you the exact grams per plant, and you should contact ICAT for any detailed dosage questions.
My maize plants have holes in the leaves and some shoots are dead.
Are the holes looking like window-pane holes on the whorl leaves?
Yes, they are like that and the central shoot is dead.

You are dealing with maize stalk borer carry over in old stalks. While the plants are young, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel; one kilogram treats about 1,500 to 2,000 plants and you must repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days. Never apply neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always mix it with an inert carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks to remove the pest source. Rotate or intercrop the field with a legume such as cowpea or soybean to break the cycle. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.
Where can I find the current live market price for my grain and who should I contact to sell it?

My yam field has some rocks and hasn't been used much. Which ground should I pick for the mounds?

Pick a place with deep, rested soil that has no stones, and that has stayed fallow for at least five years, or use a Mucuna fallow if the plot is small. Then raise mounds 40-80 cm tall, laying them about 1.4 x 1.4 m apart on good soil or 1 x 1.5 m on poorer soil, targeting roughly 5,000 or 6,500 mounds per hectare respectively. After the mounds are ready, set healthy seed setts whose cut ends have healed in shade and coat them with wood ash before planting. Stake the vines as they grow and do the first weeding at the proper time. For a suitable variety, visit ICAT or ITRA.
My field was left fallow for four years and has stones. Is it okay for yam planting on mounds?

The soil must be deep, rested and free of stones, and it should have been fallow for at least five years; if you cannot wait, sow a Mucuna cover first on the limited plot. Then raise mounds 40-80 cm high, placing them 1.4 x 1.4 m apart on fertile soil or 1 x 1.5 m on less fertile soil, targeting roughly 5,000 mounds per hectare on rich land and 6,500 on poorer land. After the mounds are ready, put healthy seed setts whose cut ends have healed in shade and dust them with wood ash before planting. Stake the vines and carry out the first weeding at the prescribed time. For a proper storage variety, consult ICAT or ITRA.
My cassava field got sick, can I plant something else there next season?

You should rotate the plot after cassava bacterial blight. First, pull out and destroy any diseased plants. Then clean your tools between each plant you handle. Next, plant a resistant cassava variety only using cuttings taken from healthy plants. After that, grow a different crop on the same land before you return to cassava. For clean resistant cuttings, see ITRA or a registered producer, and you may ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
The leaves are wilting and have spots, should I change the crop next year?

Cassava bacterial blight requires you to rotate the field. Begin by removing and destroying the affected cassava plants. Disinfect your cutting tools after each plant. Use only healthy-plant cuttings to start a new resistant cassava variety, but first plant another crop in that plot. When you need clean resistant cuttings, go to ITRA or a registered producer, and you can consult ICAT for diagnosis confirmation.
After the disease hit my cassava, can I plant the same thing again?

You must rotate the area where cassava bacterial blight occurred. First, eliminate and destroy all infected plants. Clean your tools between each plant to avoid spreading the bacterium. Then obtain cuttings from healthy plants and choose a resistant cassava type, but plant a different crop in that field before returning to cassava. For clean resistant cuttings, contact ITRA or a registered producer, and you may request ICAT to verify the disease.
What do I do with my cassava field that has gum on the stems?

The field should be rotated because of cassava bacterial blight. Start by pulling out and destroying the gum-exuding plants. Disinfect each tool after you work on a plant. Only use cuttings from healthy plants to establish a resistant cassava variety, and first grow another crop on that land before re-planting cassava. For clean resistant cuttings, visit ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
After the rain, my cassava leaves have angular wet spots and the young leaves wilt, and some stems leak gum. How should I act?

Cassava bacterial blight moves with infected cassava stems, cuttings, dirty tools and rain splash. Take cuttings only from cassava that looks healthy. Remove and destroy every cassava plant that shows the symptoms. Disinfect your cutting tools between each cassava plant you handle. Choose a resistant cassava variety and rotate the field to another site. Clean resistant cuttings are available from ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can verify the diagnosis.
The rain has been heavy and now my cassava shows wilting leaves and gum on the stems. What steps must I follow?

The cassava bacterial blight spreads through moving diseased cassava stems, contaminated cuttings, tools and rain splash. Only cuttings from healthy cassava should be used. Immediately pull out and destroy any cassava with wilting leaves or gum. Disinfect every tool before you move to the next cassava plant. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot elsewhere. For clean resistant cassava cuttings, go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the disease.
My cassava field got wet from rain and now the leaves have angular spots and the shoots are dying. What do I need to do?

Cassava bacterial blight is carried by diseased cassava stems, cuttings, tools and by rain splash. Use cuttings exclusively from cassava that looks healthy. Remove and destroy any cassava plant showing the angular spots or dying shoots. Clean and disinfect each tool before you handle another cassava plant. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the area to a new site. Clean resistant cuttings can be obtained from ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can help confirm the disease.
After a storm, my cassava leaves are wilting and the stems are oozing gum. How can I stop this disease from spreading?

The cassava bacterial blight spreads when diseased cassava stems, cuttings, tools are moved and when rain splashes the bacteria. Take cuttings only from cassava that shows no symptoms. Pull out and destroy every cassava plant that has wilting leaves or gum. Disinfect your tools between each cassava plant you work on. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to a different field. For clean resistant cuttings, see ITRA or a registered producer, and you may ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
My cassava leaves are yellowish with weird shapes, can I still harvest them?

Those symptoms mean cassava mosaic disease is present and the affected plants must be removed. Pull out the strongly mottled and stunted cassava plants and destroy them because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next planting, cut only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no leaf distortion, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Then plant an improved tolerant cassava variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer to keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.
The cassava in my field looks twisted and pale, what should I do before the next rainy season?

Twisted and pale leaves show cassava mosaic disease, so the infected cassava must be uprooted and destroyed. Remove the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. When you re-plant, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava plants with normal green leaves, avoiding any mottled or deformed stems. After you have clean cuttings, plant an improved tolerant cassava variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer to maintain a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, go to ITRA.
Is there a way to stop the spread of the leaf spots on my cassava without using chemicals?

Leaf spots with distortion indicate cassava mosaic disease, and no spray can cure it, so the infected cassava must be uprooted and destroyed. Pull out the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next crop, cut only from cassava plants that look healthy, with normal green leaves and no deformation, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Then plant an improved tolerant cassava variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer to keep a uniform, well-fed stand. To obtain clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.
The leaves of my groundnut are showing dark spots and falling off before harvest. What steps must I follow?

Those symptoms indicate groundnut leaf spot. First, clear all old groundnut residues and bury them before you sow again. Next, do not grow groundnut on that same plot in the following year; rotate it with cereals. Choose a tolerant groundnut variety for the next planting. Harvest the crop at the right time so the plants stay strong and do not drop pods early. By doing these things you limit the Cercospora leaf-spot fungi that persist in crop residues. For information on resistant varieties or fungicide decisions, consult ICAT.
After the storm, my maize looks like it's choking, the lower leaves turn pale but there are no spots. What is happening?

The pale lower leaves after the rain mean the soil is waterlogged and the roots are lacking air. First dig a shallow drainage channel so water can leave the plot instead of standing. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burn. Then keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, see ICAT.
My maize field got flooded and now the bottom leaves are turning yellow without any disease signs. What should I do?

Yellowing of the lower leaves after flooding shows the soil is waterlogged and the maize roots are being starved of air. Open a shallow drainage channel to let excess water run off the plot. After the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping it off the plant so it does not burn. Continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as planned. If streaks or dead-hearts appear, go to ICAT.
The borer seems to stay in the cut stalks after I finish my maize. How can I stop it from coming back next season?

The maize stalk borer can survive in the old stalks that remain after harvest. Immediately after you cut the maize, destroy the remaining stalks or bury them deep so the larvae cannot live in them. Then, plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same plot to break the pest cycle. Rotate or intercrop with the legume right after the old stalks are removed. While the new plants are still young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel and repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days. Use only the powder-carrier mix because neem alone can scorch the seedlings. If a large block of your field is suddenly attacked, go to ICAT quickly for approved control. Why are my young chili plants falling flat on the soil surface in the nursery?

Your chili pepper seedlings are experiencing damping-off because the beds are too wet and lack air. Water the bed so it stays evenly moist but never soggy, and stop watering late in the evening. Plant treated seed that carries a fungicide-insecticide coating and space the sowing thin enough to avoid crowding. Pull out any seedlings that have collapsed and work on better drainage and airflow in the bed. If the problem continues to spread, go to ICAT for an approved nursery drench and the correct rate.
The pepper sprouts I sowed are turning upside down at the ground level, what's happening?

Your pepper seedlings are being hit by damping-off, a fungus that thrives in wet, airless beds. Keep the seedbed evenly moist but not soggy, and do not water late in the evening so moisture does not linger overnight. Use seed that has been treated with a fungicide-insecticide coat and do not sow them too thickly. Remove any seedlings that have toppled, and improve the bed's drainage and airflow. If the disease keeps moving through the bed, visit ICAT for an approved nursery drench and the proper application rate.
My chili seedlings are collapsing right at the soil line; could it be a water problem?

The little pepper plants I planted are lying flat and breaking at the base, is this normal?

If the situation keeps getting worse, go to ICAT for an approved nursery drench and the correct dosage.
Why do my chili seedling rows have plants that tip over and die at soil level?

Plant treated seed with a fungicide-insecticide coat and sow them thin enough to avoid overcrowding. Pull out any seedlings that have collapsed and enhance drainage and airflow in the nursery. My pigs keep getting sick and I see red spots on their ears. What should I do to stop the disease from spreading?

The problem is African swine fever on pigs. First, clean and disinfect the whole pen thoroughly to remove the virus. Then set up a footbath filled with disinfectant at the pen entrance so anyone entering steps in a clean solution. After that, boil all food scraps you plan to give the pigs before feeding them, because swill can carry the virus. These actions target the ways African swine fever on pigs spreads. Finally, contact the veterinary service right away for notification and further guidance.
I heard my neighbour's pigs died fast from a strange fever. How can I protect my herd?

You are dealing with African swine fever on pigs. Begin by disinfecting the pig pen completely to kill any virus present. Next, place a disinfectant footbath at the gate of the pen so boots and shoes are cleaned before entry. Then, any kitchen leftovers or swill must be boiled before you feed them to the pigs, as this prevents virus transmission. These steps address the main routes of African swine fever on pigs spread. After doing this, notify the veterinary service immediately.
My pig pen is always dirty and I feed them leftovers. Is that why they are dying so fast?

The disease you are seeing is African swine fever on pigs. You need to disinfect the entire pen to eliminate the virus from surfaces. Install a disinfectant footbath at the pen entrance so anyone coming in cleans their footwear. Boil all food scraps before giving them to the pigs, because untreated swill can spread African swine fever on pigs. These measures stop the virus from moving via contact, boots, clothes, and feed. Then, report the situation to the veterinary service without delay.
My coop is near a ditch that holds water after rain and I think mosquitoes are making my chickens sick. What can I do?

Mosquitoes breeding in standing water help spread fowl pox, so you must eliminate any puddles around the coop. First, separate any chickens that show raised, wart-like scabs on their combs, wattles or face from the healthy birds. Then give the isolated birds extra feed and clean water while the dry form of fowl pox runs its mild course. After that, drain or fill any standing water and keep the area around the coop tidy to cut down mosquito numbers. When the affected chickens recover, arrange vaccination for the whole flock against fowl pox. For any assistance, especially with the wet form, see the veterinary service.
My chickens just lost many birds in one day, but a few are still alive. Can I sell the survivors at the market?

You must not move, sell or give any chicken after a Newcastle disease outbreak. First separate every surviving chicken from the sick ones. Then burn or bury all dead chickens together with any contaminated litter. After that, clean and disinfect the coop thoroughly. Finally give the flock the La Sota or B1 vaccine in the drinking water or as eye-drops and repeat according to the schedule. If you need assistance, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.
Several of my hens died suddenly and the rest look okay, is it safe to take the healthy ones to the market?

No, you cannot transport any chicken after a Newcastle disease episode. Begin by isolating each surviving chicken away from the infected birds. Next, burn or bury the dead chickens and any soiled bedding. Then disinfect the housing area completely. Afterwards vaccinate the entire flock with the La Sota or B1 strain using drinking water or eye-drops, following the recommended schedule. You should see the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary immediately for help.
The birds in my coop died all at once, but a couple are still breathing. May I bring those to the market?

It is not allowed to move, sell or give any chicken after a Newcastle disease incident. First, isolate every remaining chicken from the diseased ones. Then burn or bury the dead chickens and any contaminated litter. Clean the coop and apply disinfectant to the whole house. Finally, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 vaccine in the water or as eye-drops, repeating as scheduled. Seek assistance from the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary without delay.
My rice seedlings are getting sick, could it be from the seed I used?

Rice blast can be carried on seed, so you must treat the seed before sowing. First, avoid applying too much nitrogen by splitting urea and staying within the recommended dose. Then treat the seed you will sow next season with a Fongorene-type product at 6 g per kg of seed. If the disease is already severe, use an approved benomyl-type fungicide at about 500 g per hectare, improve drainage and airflow, and plant a tolerant variety. For the current approved fungicide and exact rate, go to ICAT.
Is the blast disease in my rice coming from the seed I bought?

Rice blast is indeed spread on seed, so seed treatment is essential. Begin by stopping any over-application of nitrogen, split urea doses and do not exceed the recommended amount. Next, treat next season's seed with a Fongorene-type product at 6 g per kg of seed. If you face a bad outbreak, apply an approved benomyl-type fungicide at roughly 500 g per hectare, improve field drainage and airflow, and use a tolerant rice variety. To obtain the current approved fungicide and correct dosage, consult ICAT.
Can the rice blast problem be linked to the seed I planted last year?

Rice blast can be carried on seed, so you should treat the seed before planting. First step is to stop over-applying nitrogen by splitting urea applications and respecting the recommended dose. Then treat the seed you will use next season with a Fongorene-type at 6 g per kg of seed. If the outbreak is serious, apply an approved benomyl-type fungicide at about 500 g per hectare, improve drainage and airflow, and select a tolerant variety. For the current approved fungicide and exact rate, visit ICAT.
My rice field is getting blast, could the seed be the source?

Afterwards, treat the seed you will sow next season with a Fongorene-type product at 6 g per kg of seed. My cow's left side is puffed up like a drum and she won't eat, is this something contagious?

Your cow has bloat and it is not infectious. First, make her stand and walk while holding her head up so she can try to belch. Next, give a small drench of vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth and let the gas out. After you have done these actions, call the veterinary service straight away for emergency help.
I saw my goat's flank swell and he is breathing hard after the rain started, what is this problem?

The goat is suffering from bloat, which does not spread to other animals. Quickly get the goat moving and keep its head raised to aid belching. Then administer a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to dissolve the froth and release the trapped gas. Once these steps are taken, contact the veterinary service immediately for urgent treatment.
My sheep stopped eating and its left side is tight and swollen after we switched to a legume field, what should I do?

That is bloat and it is not contagious. Immediately get the sheep up and walking while keeping its head lifted to encourage belching. Follow by drenching a small amount of vegetable or mineral oil into its mouth to break the froth and allow gas to escape. After performing these measures, call the veterinary service right away for emergency assistance.
My tomatoes are getting a strange disease, the leaves look wet and black and the fruit rots fast. Who is causing this?

The pathogen behind tomato late blight is the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Cut off any leaves, stems or whole tomato plants that show those dark, water-soaked lesions and destroy them right away. After removal, spread out the remaining tomato plants and put stakes in place so air can move through the canopy. Do not water the tomatoes from overhead late in the day to keep the foliage dry. Plant a tomato variety that is known to be resistant to late blight for the next cycle. If you still need chemical help, obtain an approved fungicide and apply it at the labelled rate, which you can get from ICAT.
There is a white mould on the underside of my tomato leaves and the leaves are collapsing. What organism is responsible?

Tomato late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Immediately remove and destroy any tomato leaves, stems or plants that carry the white mould and water-soaked lesions. Then arrange the remaining tomato plants with proper spacing and stake them to improve airflow inside the canopy. Avoid watering from overhead late in the day to reduce humidity on the leaves. Choose a resistant tomato variety for future plantings. For any needed fungicide, go to ICAT to get the approved product and follow the label rate.
The leaves on my tomato plants are wilting and the fruit is rotting, how should I arrange my garden?

You are dealing with tomato late blight, so rearrange your garden to improve ventilation. First, set each tomato plant at a spacing that leaves clear gaps for wind to move through the canopy. Then, insert a sturdy stake for every plant at planting and fasten the vines to keep them vertical. This reduces the crowded, humid conditions that let spores move. Avoid watering overhead late in the day; apply water directly to the soil with drip or a watering can at the base. Cut off any leaf or stem with dark, water-soaked lesions and destroy them promptly. Plant a resistant tomato variety and, if needed, treat with an approved fungicide at the labelled rate. To obtain the right fungicide and its rate, consult ICAT.
The tomato leaves in my garden are yellow and curling upward, and I get almost no fruit. How should I treat these plants?

Rogue out the badly affected tomato plants right away. Begin by identifying all tomato plants that display upward curling, yellow leaves, stunted bushy growth and poor fruit set. Remove each identified plant from the garden and destroy it to stop further spread. Then keep the garden clean and act early to control any whitefly present, the vector of tomato yellow leaf curl virus. Plant a resistant tomato variety for your next crop. For help with whitefly management and resistant varieties, see ICAT.
I see some of my tomato leaves are yellow and curled upward, and the plants are very short. What is the correct action?

The correct action is to rogue out the badly affected tomato plants. First, scout your garden for tomato plants with upward curling, yellowing leaves, stunted bushy growth and poor fruit set. Pull those plants out and destroy them to prevent the virus from spreading. Afterwards, keep the plot clean and act early to control whitefly, which carries tomato yellow leaf curl virus. Use a resistant tomato variety for the next planting season. For guidance on whitefly control and resistant seeds, contact ICAT.
I have grain to sell. Which national service deals with grain sales and food security?

ANSAT. That is the service concerned with grain sales and food security, and it is the one to approach for that question rather than any other. grain to sell. which service?

Three different bodies, three different jobs, and putting the wrong name in front of a buyer costs you a trip.
ANSAT or INSEED for my grain?

ANSAT for the grain itself. It is the service concerned with grain sales and food security. INSEED tracks prices, which is useful background but not the body you approach to sell. I have thirty bags in store and I want to move them before the prices drop.

Why not just take my grain to any buyer at the market?

You can, and often that is exactly right. The reason to know the services is that the market price on one day in one place is not the whole picture. What price will ANSAT give me for my maize?

Name every service you know for selling, and say what each one does.

Four, and each does a different thing. ANSAT is concerned with grain sales and food security. INSEED tracks prices. The Direction du Commerce Exterieur handles exports. SIM is where cereal prices are broadcast on the radio, which is how you compare markets before selling. Alongside those, a cooperative or ICAT helps you reach larger buyers than you would alone. I would not stretch any of them beyond that: each name goes with one job.
I am going to sell tomorrow. What should I have done first?

Three things, and none of them takes long. Follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio so you know what the grain is worth before anyone makes you an offer. Compare the local price plus transport against an urban market, because carrying grain only pays if the difference covers the journey and the handling. And if you can sell as a group or through a cooperative, do it, because that reaches bigger buyers and cuts the cost per bag. For the grain sales and food security side, ANSAT is the service concerned.
Just give me one name and I will go there.

ANSAT, if the question is grain sales and food security. That is the one service concerned with that side, so it is the single name I would give you. But before you travel, spend ten minutes on the price: follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio and compare the local price plus transport against an urban market. It costs nothing and it decides whether the trip is worth making at all.
Which body handles exports, if I wanted to sell outside Togo?

The Direction du Commerce Exterieur. That is the one for exports. It is not the same as ANSAT, which is concerned with grain sales and food security inside the country, and not the same as INSEED, which tracks prices. Before any of that, the local calculation still applies: compare the local price plus transport against the market you are thinking of, because the further the grain travels the more the handling eats into what you keep.
